#PatrickStewart is being mourned by Marvel Studios and Kevin Feige following his death at 86 years old.
https://variety.com/2026/film/news/patrick-stewart-death-marvel-kevin-feige-tributes-x-men-1236934424/

"I’ll never forget the first time I saw Sir Patrick Stewart on the set of the first 'X-Men,'" Feige writes in an emotional tribute. "After years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas. Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed."

Marvel Studios adds: "We're deeply saddened by the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart. Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from X- Men to Logan to Avengers: Doomsday. He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman. Our hearts go out to his wife Sunny, his children, his friends, and the countless fans around the world whose lives he touched with his art."

REMEMBERING PATRICK STEWART

Patrick Stewart, the legendary actor best known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, has died at 86.

His family said in a statement: "We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia." 

"His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre.  He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise... He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role - in his art and life."

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

Known as "The Saints," the RLI was a light infantry commando battalion that built its reputation during the Rhodesian Bush War, and is still often discussed among the most effective counterinsurgency units of its era.

Its fame came from Fireforce, a rapid reaction tactic in which small groups of soldiers were flown into contact by helicopter, often supported by paratroopers dropped from Dakotas, to surround and engage insurgent groups within minutes of them being spotted. At the height of the war, RLI troopers could find themselves deployed into action several times in a short period, and many made combat parachute jumps far more often than soldiers in most modern armies.

The FN FAL was their standard rifle, a reliable 7.62mm battle rifle well suited to the open bush and the close, fast engagements that Fireforce produced.

This illustration shows the kind of concealed sniper positions the Viet Cong used throughout the Vietnam War. Often called "spider holes," these were small, one man fighting positions dug into the ground, covered with a camouflaged lid made of wood, leaves, and soil, so they blended almost perfectly into the surrounding terrain.

A sniper could wait inside for hours, lift the cover just enough to take a shot, and then disappear again before anyone could locate where the fire had come from. Some positions were connected to tunnel networks, allowing the shooter to move away underground while American troops searched the area above.

For U.S. and allied forces, the threat shaped how they patrolled. Every clearing, trail, and tree line had the potential to hide a shooter who could not be seen until it was too late. It was a simple, low tech solution that proved deadly effective against a far better equipped enemy.

Not one Comanche transmission was ever understood by the enemy. Seventeen men did that. Charles Joyce Chibitty was a Comanche kid from near Medicine Park, Oklahoma, when the Army came looking for men who spoke his language. He became one of just seventeen Comanche code talkers assigned to the 4th Infantry Division — a tiny band of men carrying an outsized secret into the biggest invasion in history.

On the morning of June 6, 1944, Chibitty came ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, among the very first code talkers to put the language to work in Europe. Chibitty fought through the whole campaign and came home to Oklahoma, where in his later years he became the honored elder of the Comanche code talkers — traveling, teaching, and reminding America that Native men had helped win the war in a voice straight from their own grandmothers' kitchens. Honors found him at last, including the Army's Knowlton Award for intelligence work. The code talkers did not begin in World War II. They began in France, in 1918. 🇺🇸

In October 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the American 36th Division had a deadly problem: German listeners tapped their phone lines at will, and every code the Americans tried was broken within hours. Then an officer overheard two of his own soldiers chatting in Choctaw — and realized he was listening to a language no German on Earth could understand.

Within days, Choctaw soldiers of the 141st Infantry were manning field telephones across the sector, relaying orders for troop movements and artillery in their native tongue. In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

In a historic ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit struck down core provisions of the 1958 Federal Switchblade Act, holding that automatically opening knives qualify as protected "Arms" under the plain text of the Second Amendment.

Dismantling a 1950s Ban: Enacted in 1958 amid 1950s pop-culture panics over juvenile delinquency, Section 1242 of the Federal Switchblade Act made it a federal crime to manufacture, transport, or sell automatic knives across state lines. The appellate panel found that the federal government failed to demonstrate any historical tradition justifying an interstate commercial ban.

Knives Are Constitutionally Protected "Arms": Applying the Supreme Court's historical-tradition framework, Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod wrote for the panel that bladed tools have been used for self-defense throughout American history. The court explicitly held that the right to keep and bear arms necessarily includes the right to manufacture, ship, and acquire them through interstate commerce.

What Changes (and What Doesn't): While the decision represents a major victory for pro-knife advocacy groups like Knife Rights and clears federal interstate trade barriers within the circuit, it does not automatically override individual state or municipal concealed-carry and blade-length statutes, which remain governed under separate local laws.

They called him unbroken — and after 47 days at sea and two years in the camps, the name fit. 🇺🇸

Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner from California who raced at the 1936 Berlin Games, and when war came he became a bombardier on a B-24 over the Pacific. On May 27, 1943, his crippled bomber, the Green Hornet, fell into the ocean during a rescue search. Zamperini and two crewmates survived on a tiny raft — drinking rain, catching fish and birds, fending off sharks — for 47 days, among the longest sea survivals in history. One of the three died on the raft. The other two washed up alive — straight into Japanese hands.

What followed was worse than the ocean: more than two years in prisoner-of-war camps, singled out for torment by a sadistic guard the prisoners called "the Bird," who beat the famous Olympian with a belt, starved him, and tried to break the thing in him that would not bend. It never broke. Zamperini came home in 1945 carrying nightmares that nearly destroyed him with drink — until, by his own account, faith put him back together, and the man who had every reason to hate flew back to Japan to forgive his captors face to face.

He died in 2014 at 97, a torch-bearer, a mentor to generations of young men, and the subject of the book and film "Unbroken." The title is not poetry. It is a description.

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. By July 2, 1863, he commanded the 20th Maine — and held the extreme left end of the entire Union line on Little Round Top at Gettysburg, with orders to hold "to the last." Among the officers beside him was his younger brother, Lieutenant Thomas Chamberlain.

All afternoon the 20th Maine beat back wave after wave of Alabamians climbing the rocks. Then the ammunition ran out. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. He was wounded so often in that war that newspapers printed his obituary by mistake; Grant chose him to formally receive the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, where Chamberlain ordered his men to salute their defeated enemies as they stacked their arms.

Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Can modern forensic breakthroughs finally bring closure to families more than five decades after one of America's most notorious serial killers struck?

Summit County, Utah prosecutors and law enforcement officials have formally linked infamous serial killer Ted Bundy to the unsolved October 1974 murder of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith through advanced DNA testing.

A 52-Year Cold Case Solved: Melissa Ann Smith disappeared in late October 1974, and her body was later discovered in Summit County by hunters. For decades, her murder remained officially unsolved despite long-standing suspicions regarding Bundy's presence in Utah while attending law school.

The Forensics Breakthrough: Investigators closed the case after connecting genetic evidence preserved from Smith's autopsy to DNA profiles established in the case of Laura Aime—another 17-year-old Utah victim whose murder was definitively tied to Bundy through DNA earlier this year.

Closing the Book on Unsolved Victims: Executed in Florida's electric chair in 1989, Bundy confessed to dozens of killings across Washington, Utah, Colorado, Idaho, and Florida, though several remained unconfirmed. Utah investigators emphasized that every cold case closure helps bring answers to surviving families while bringing permanent resolution to his trail of crimes.

Two brothers of one Wisconsin family — and between them, two of the Civil War's most impossible feats. 🇺🇸

Alonzo Cushing, pictured here, was a 22-year-old artillery lieutenant whose battery stood at the very center of the Union line at Gettysburg — the stone wall called the Angle — on July 3, 1863. As Pickett's Charge rolled toward him, Alonzo was wounded again and again: a shell fragment through the shoulder, another through the body. Ordered to the rear, he refused, had himself held upright beside his last serviceable gun, and was sighting it with his thumb over the vent when a bullet struck him down at his post. The charge broke on the ground he would not leave. In November 2014 — 151 years later — President Barack Obama placed Alonzo Cushing's Medal of Honor where it had always belonged.

His younger brother needed no land battle for his legend. William Barker Cushing of the U.S. Navy, on the night of October 27, 1864, steamed a tiny launch with a spar torpedo up the dark Roanoke River, alone past Confederate guards, and detonated it beneath the ironclad CSS Albemarle — sinking the South's most feared warship and swimming for his life through icy water as it went down.

One brother held the line at the war's turning point. The other sank an ironclad in the dark. America has rarely asked more of one family's sons — and never received more.

The Federal Election Commission (FEC) reporting and filing network has been knocked offline following a suspected cyber incident, severely interrupting the flow of public campaign finance records and 48-hour late-contribution disclosures ahead of national voting.

 Agency databases and electronic submission portals went dark following what cybersecurity officials describe as an external distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) incident and network intrusion attempt, preventing campaigns and PACs from submitting mandated last-minute financial reports.

The outage strikes during the single highest-volume reporting window of the election cycle, blinding oversight groups, reporters, and the public to tens of millions of dollars in final campaign contributions pouring into critical battleground races.

 CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and federal investigators have stepped in to isolate agency servers, trace potential foreign or domestic threat actors, and restore secure access while issuing emergency paper-filing extensions for affected political committees.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

This is the true story behind Saving Private Ryan — and the truth is harder than the film. 🇺🇸

Four brothers from Tonawanda, New York, went to war: Edward, Preston, Robert and Frederick "Fritz" Niland. In one terrible June of 1944, the family's world collapsed. Robert, a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne, was k*lled on D-Day itself at Neuville-au-Plain. The very next day, June 7, Preston, also a paratrooper, fell near Utah Beach. And from the other side of the world came word that Edward, an airman whose plane had gone down in the Burmese jungle, was missing and presumed d*ad.

That left Fritz, fighting with the 101st Airborne in Normandy. When the Army realized three brothers were gone, it moved fast: the regimental chaplain, Father Francis Sampson, tracked Fritz down and the last Niland son was pulled from the line and sent home to his mother — the real "sole survivor" mission that Steven Spielberg later transformed into Saving Private Ryan.

And then, in 1945, came the telegram no one dared hope for: Edward was alive. Emaciated in a Japanese prison camp, he had survived. Two Niland brothers came home. Two rest side by side today in the American cemetery above Normandy — Preston and Robert, together, under white crosses in Plot B.

Five brothers. One ship. One night that changed America's rules of war forever. 🇺🇸

George, Francis, Joseph, Madison and Albert Sullivan were five Irish-American brothers from Waterloo, Iowa. When their friend Bill Ball was k*lled aboard the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, the brothers enlisted together — with one condition the Navy granted: they would serve together. All five were posted to the light cruiser USS Juneau, and their smiling photograph aboard her became one of the famous images of the young war.

On the night of November 13, 1942, in the savage naval battles off Guadalcanal, a Japanese torpedo struck the Juneau's magazine. She disintegrated and sank in less than a minute. Some hundred men survived the sinking and clung to rafts in shark-haunted water — but through a chain of communication failures, no rescue came for days. When help finally arrived, only ten men were pulled out alive. All five Sullivan brothers were gone.

Their mother Alleta received the news with a grace that humbled a nation, and their sister Genevieve joined the Navy's WAVES in their honor. The Navy named a destroyer USS The Sullivans — the only American warship ever named for a family — and the tragedy drove the military to separate siblings and protect sole surviving sons. "We stick together" was the brothers' motto. They did — to the very end.

Before there was a 75th Ranger Regiment, there was one young colonel in Scotland, building America's first Rangers from scratch. 🇺🇸

In the spring of 1942, with America reeling from defeats, Major William Orlando Darby — just 31 years old — was given a mission: create an American unit modeled on the legendary British Commandos. Five hundred volunteers were selected and shipped to Achnacarry, Scotland, where Commando instructors ran them through a course so brutal it used live ammunition. On June 19, 1942, the 1st Ranger Battalion was born — and Darby's men, pictured training here in those early days, were its standard-bearers.

That November, Rangers spearheaded the landings in North Africa, paddling ashore in darkness to silence the guns of Arzew. They fought through Sicily and Italy, at Gela and Salerno and Anzio — and at Cisterna, in January 1944, the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions walked into an ambush and were nearly annihilated: of 767 men who went in, only six came back.

Darby refused a safe job in Washington and returned to his men in Italy. On April 30, 1945, days before the war in Europe ended, a shell fragment took his life; he was promoted to Brigadier General on the day of his death. Today's Rangers still carry his name, his scroll, and his challenge — Darby's challenge — to lead the way. Rangers Lead The Way.

This U.S. soldier's M16A1 has one of the strangest attachments of the Vietnam War: the XM2 personnel detector, better known to the troops as the "People Sniffer." Developed by General Electric for the Army's Chemical Corps and fielded in 1967, it was built to find an enemy that was nearly impossible to see in thick jungle by detecting the chemical traces of human sweat and urine.

The system had a sensor carried in a backpack and an air intake tube mounted at the end of the rifle. Wherever the muzzle pointed, the device sampled the air. In theory, it would lead a patrol straight to a hidden enemy position.

In practice, troops found plenty of problems. The detector made noise, which is the last thing you want in an ambush position, and it was sensitive enough to pick up the sweat of the soldiers carrying it. The enemy also adapted quickly, reportedly hanging buckets of urine in the jungle to send the sniffers chasing ghosts. The airborne XM3 version mounted on helicopters saw much wider use, but the backpack model became a footnote.

It's a strange piece of gear and a reminder of how hard American troops worked to find an enemy who rarely wanted to be found.

The enemy kept a diary about them. One word appears again and again: the Black Devils. 🇺🇸

The First Special Service Force was an experiment no army had tried: one elite unit of Americans and Canadians, mixed together, trained for everything — parachuting, skiing, mountain climbing, amphibious raids, demolitions — at a secret camp in Montana under Colonel Robert Frederick.

In December 1943, at Monte la Difensa in Italy, the Force did what Allied planners called impossible: in a freezing night rainstorm, its men scaled a sheer cliff the Germans had left undefended precisely because no one could climb it — and took the summit fortress in two hours. At the Anzio beachhead, they owned the night: faces blackened, slipping into German lines to raid, sabotage and vanish, leaving behind their red spearhead sticker and a calling card in German: "Das dicke Ende kommt noch!" — "The worst is yet to come!"

A captured German officer's diary gave them their immortal name, describing an enemy that struck invisibly in the dark: "the Black Devils." The Force was disbanded in December 1944, its ranks shattered by casualties — but both nations' special forces trace their bloodline to it. The Devil's Brigade never lost a battle it was sent to win.

Can Ukrainian frontline units hold the line as the Pokrovsk sector erupts into one of the most violently contested axes of the entire war?

According to daily operational updates from the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Ukrainian defenders repelled 36 Russian assaults in the Pokrovsk sector alone, amid a relentless operational surge that recorded 177 combat clashes across the front line in a single 24-hour period.

The Pokrovsk direction continues to absorb the heaviest concentration of adversary armored thrusts and infantry assaults, as Russian forces press aggressively to compromise vital logistical lifelines in Donetsk Oblast.

Despite heavy artillery preparatory bombardments, guided glide bombs (KABs), and continuous mechanized waves, Ukrainian artillery, anti-tank teams, and FPV drone operators successfully blunted all 36 targeted assault vectors.

While the Pokrovsk sector remains the hottest contact zone on the map, intense localized fighting also stretched defenders across the Lyman, Kostiantynivka, and Huliaipole fronts, underscoring the grueling operational tempo spanning hundreds of miles.
No shortcuts. No excuses. Just disciplined fires and reps that build readiness.

America locked their families behind barbed wire — then these sons volunteered to fight for it. 🇺🇸

After Pearl Harbor, more than 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced from their homes into internment camps. And from inside those camps, thousands of their sons stepped forward and volunteered for the United States Army. They became the 442nd Regimental Combat Team — fighting under a motto in Hawaiian pidgin: "Go For Broke."

In Italy and France, the 442nd built a legend battle by battle. In October 1944, in the freezing Vosges Mountains, they smashed through German lines to rescue the "Lost Battalion" — 211 trapped Texans of the 141st Infantry — at a cost of some 800 casualties of their own. Their artillerymen, like the 522nd Field Artillery gunners pictured here under their camouflage net, were famed for speed and precision — and in the spring of 1945, men of the 522nd were among the liberators who reached the sub-camps of Dachau.

For its size and length of service, the 442nd became the most decorated unit in United States Army history: more than 18,000 individual decorations, including 21 Medals of Honor. They had set out to prove their loyalty to a country that doubted it. They ended up proving something greater — what loyalty actually looks like.

The U.S. Navy embraces Castelion's low-cost "Blackbeard" hypersonic missile to counter complex anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) networks.

As defense leaders shift focus toward high-end conventional deterrence in the Indo-Pacific, the U.S. military is rapidly accelerating the development and fielding of mass-producible, high-speed strike weapons designed to outpace adversary defensive perimeters.

 Developed by defense startup Castelion, the Blackbeard (selected under the Navy's Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector or MACE initiative) is an air-launched, long-range hypersonic weapon capable of speeds exceeding Mach 4 to Mach 5-plus.

 Unlike multi-million-dollar legacy hypersonics, Blackbeard is engineered specifically for mass production, with initial pre-production batches priced around $468,000 and long-term targets aiming under $300,000 per unit.

 Designed to integrate seamlessly with carrier air wings aboard platforms like the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and F-35, the weapon allows strike fighters to hold high-value mobile and time-sensitive targets at risk from far outside adversary A2/AD missile engagement zones.

They marched a thousand miles through jungle, fought an empire, and dissolved almost to the last man. 🇺🇸

In February 1944, some 3,000 American volunteers — jungle fighters, muleskinners, and men who spoke languages of the Pacific — slipped behind Japanese lines in Burma. Officially they were the 5307th Composite Unit. History knows them by their commander, Brigadier General Frank Merrill: Merrill's Marauders.

With only what they and their mules could carry, they marched farther than any American unit of the war — some 750 to 1,000 miles of mountain and jungle — and fought five major battles and dozens of skirmishes, cutting the supply lines of an army that outnumbered them many times over. Their true enemies were as much malaria, dysentery, and scrub typhus as the Japanese: men fought with fevers of 104 degrees, and the wounded who could walk were sent back to the line.

When the airfield at Myitkyina finally fell in August 1944, of the nearly 3,000 who had marched in, only about 200 remained fit for duty. Every Marauder received the Bronze Star, and in 2020 Congress awarded the unit its Gold Medal. Their legacy marches on today in the 75th Ranger Regiment, which carries the Marauders' lineage — and their impossible standard.

The operator standing near the center in the "daisy dukes" and white T-shirt is Special Warfare Operator 2nd Class (SEAL) David J. Warsen of SEAL Team 3. Known as "Davey" to those closest to him, he was killed in action on August 16, 2012, when the Black Hawk he was riding in was shot down by a rocket propelled grenade northeast of Kandahar, Afghanistan.

Davey grew up in Kentwood, Michigan, and graduated from East Kentwood High School. He enlisted in the Navy in March 2009 and graduated from BUD/S a year later. Family members remembered him as an upbeat guy who was incredibly proud to be a SEAL and worked hard for it. His deployment was scheduled to end on October 1, and he and his fiancée, Karlyn, had planned to marry that December.

He was 27 years old. Six other Americans and four Afghans were also lost in the crash, including his teammate, SO1 (SEAL) Patrick Feeks. Today, a stretch of M-6 near his hometown carries his name, and each year his family and community gather to keep his legacy alive.

What happens when a handful of CIA operatives and Green Berets infiltrate the Hindu Kush on horseback to rewrite the playbook of modern unconventional warfare?

Remembering the legendary operators of Task Force Dagger—including CIA Special Activities Division (SAD) officers and U.S. Army Special Forces from ODA 595—who dropped into northern Afghanistan in October 2001 to launch America's retaliation just weeks after the 9/11 attacks.

Operating deep behind enemy lines in harsh, mountainous terrain with zero infrastructure, these teams linked up with Northern Alliance warlords like General Abdul Rashid Dostum. To traverse the rugged, roadless cliffs, they famously adapted by riding on horseback alongside local fighters, earning the immortal moniker "The Horse Soldiers."

 While riding horses across ancient trails, these operators carried cutting-edge satellite communications and laser designators. They coordinated devastating, precision air strikes from B-52s and F-18s directly onto Taliban and Al-Qaeda positions, turning indigenous cavalry charges into an unstoppable modern fighting force.

Their daring mission resulted in the historic capture of Mazar-i-Sharif, shattering Taliban control in the north and setting the stage for the opening chapters of Operation Enduring Freedom. Their extraordinary story was later immortalized in the book and film 12 Strong.

Their tanks were rubber. Their guns were dummies. And they saved thousands of lives. Meet the Ghost Army. 🇺🇸

In the summer of 1944, a strange unit landed in France: the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops — 1,100 men recruited not for their shooting, but for their sketchbooks. They were art students, designers, actors, architects and sound engineers, and their mission was pure deception: to impersonate entire American divisions — 30,000 men — with inflatable tanks, dummy aircraft, giant speakers blasting recorded sounds of armies on the move, and fake radio traffic.

Again and again, the Ghost Army set up its theater near the front while the real divisions slipped away to attack somewhere else. German reconnaissance saw the "tanks," heard the "army," and aimed at ghosts. Historians credit the unit with saving between 15,000 and 30,000 American lives — and then the whole story was classified for half a century. The artists never got their parade.

That finally changed on March 21, 2024, when the surviving Ghost Army veterans — most near a hundred years old — received the Congressional Gold Medal in Washington. One of their inflatable Sherman tanks, like the one pictured here, survives today in a museum: a balloon that helped win a war.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A U.S. Marine with 1st Battalion, 8th Marines, fires a Mk 153 Mod 0 SMAW in Fallujah, Iraq, in November 2004. During the Second Battle of Fallujah, Marines fought house to house through a city full of insurgent strongpoints, fortified buildings, and prepared fighting positions, and the SMAW became one of their most important tools.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

The U.S. Marine Corps has officially identified the 21-year-old infantryman from Minnesota who was tragically lost at sea during training operations off the coast of Southern California as Lance Corporal Armando Ortiz Canseco.

A Salvadoran soldier carries one of the more unusual rifle setups you'll ever see: an M16 fitted with an M203 grenade launcher and an M72 LAW rocket launcher mounted on top. That's a rifle, a 40mm grenade launcher, and a 66mm anti-armor rocket all in one package.

During El Salvador's civil war in the 1980s, the Salvadoran Army received large amounts of American equipment, including M16s, M203s, and M72 LAWs, which made a combination like this possible. In close fights against guerrilla forces in mountains, villages, and dense vegetation, having that much firepower within reach could make all the difference, even if mounting it all together wasn't exactly standard practice.

Whether this was a field modification or a one off experiment, it was definitely not light, and probably not great for balance.

Can a dedicated 26-Marine Scout Platoon fully replace the legendary Scout Sniper platoons and give infantry commanders the ultimate eyes and ears on the modern battlefield? 

The U.S. Marine Corps’ newest primary infantry career field—the 0315 Marine Scout—is officially in effect, establishing a dedicated reconnaissance and surveillance pipeline on the heels of the Corps' controversial decision to phase out traditional Scout Sniper platoons in 2023.   

Previously treated as an additional skillset rather than a standalone career path, Marine Scouts now hold their own Primary Military Occupational Specialty (PMOS 0315) alongside riflemen (0311), machine gunners (0331), and mortarmen (0341). 

These specially trained Marines populate a 26-Marine Scout Platoon inside each infantry battalion—as well as scout teams within Light Armored Reconnaissance (LAR) battalions. Each scout team also embeds a certified Joint Fires Observer (JFO) capable of calling in devastating air and artillery strikes on high-value enemy targets. 

Trained in advanced fieldcraft, stealth, unmanned aerial systems, and assured long-range communications, 0315 Scouts are built to slip ahead of the main force, map routes to the objective, and extend an infantry battalion's sensing capabilities across contested littoral and inland environments.

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

This illustration shows the kind of concealed sniper positions the Viet Cong used throughout the Vietnam War. Often called "spider holes," these were small, one man fighting positions dug into the ground, covered with a camouflaged lid made of wood, leaves, and soil, so they blended almost perfectly into the surrounding terrain.

A sniper could wait inside for hours, lift the cover just enough to take a shot, and then disappear again before anyone could locate where the fire had come from. Some positions were connected to tunnel networks, allowing the shooter to move away underground while American troops searched the area above.

For U.S. and allied forces, the threat shaped how they patrolled. Every clearing, trail, and tree line had the potential to hide a shooter who could not be seen until it was too late. It was a simple, low tech solution that proved deadly effective against a far better equipped enemy.

Within twenty-four hours the tide in the sector turned; within seventy-two, the surprised enemy was in full retreat — and American officers were writing reports calling the Choctaw telephone squad one of the cleverest moves of the war.

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Yet when they came home, their story was buried for decades; most Americans never learned their names in their lifetimes. It took until 2008 for Congress to formally honor them, and 2013 for their gold medals to be struck. In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

In November 1950, Lieutenant Colonel Don Carlos Faith Jr. commanded the 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, near the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Chinese forces had encircled the Americans in brutal winter cold — temperatures plunging, weapons jamming in the freeze, wounded men fighting simply to survive.

Faith refused to stay behind the lines. Again and again he exposed himself to enemy fire, directing his men and personally leading counterattacks. When his battered force linked up with another surrounded American unit, he took command of the combined group — the force history remembers as Task Force Faith — and led the desperate fight to break out toward friendly lines, roadblock after roadblock standing in the way.

On December 1, Faith led the assault on an enemy roadblock himself, advancing with his pistol and throwing grenades. Shrapnel tore into him, but he kept directing his men until the obstacle fell. He succumbed to his wounds the following day. In the chaos of the retreat, his body could not be recovered.

He was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor in 1951. His wife and his four-year-old daughter, Bobbie, accepted the decoration — with no grave to visit. In 2012, after decades of uncertainty, military specialists identified his remains through forensic evidence and DNA. On April 17, 2013, Don Faith was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery. His daughter was there. He had spent his last days fighting to bring his soldiers home — and more than six decades later, his country finally brought him home.

Sergeant Ashly Lynn Moyer grew up in Pennsylvania, graduated from Emmaus High School in 2003, and joined the Army with her whole future in front of her. Assigned to the 630th Military Police Company, she deployed to Iraq — and dreamed, like so many young soldiers, of the life waiting after the deployment: marriage, a family, coming home.

On March 3, 2007, Moyer was driving in a military convoy through Baghdad when an improvised explosive device struck her armored vehicle. She lost her life alongside two soldiers she served with, Sergeant Michael C. Peek, 23, and Sergeant Brandon A. Parr, 25 — three young lives, gone in a single blast.

Her boyfriend, fellow soldier Jake Wells, was there that day. He had planned to propose when they returned to the United States that summer. It is the kind of loss that follows a person forever.

On March 16, 2007, her family and friends laid her to rest at Arlington National Cemetery. In 2012, an Army Reserve Center in Pennsylvania was dedicated in her honor. Ashly Moyer deserves to be remembered not only for how she served, but for the future she never got to live — a daughter, a loved one, a young woman with everything still ahead of her.

In the Hanoi Hilton, the guards answered to their commanders. The prisoners answered to James Stockdale. 🇺🇸

When Commander James Stockdale's A-4 Skyhawk was shot down over North Vietnam on September 9, 1965, he became the highest-ranking American naval officer in captivity — and the leader of the prisoner resistance. From inside Hoa Lo Prison, Stockdale built an organization out of whispers and wall-taps: a code of conduct for men under torture, secret communications between cells, and one unbreakable rule — nobody cooperates, nobody bows, everybody comes home with honor.

The North Vietnamese isolated him for it: years in solitary, long stretches in leg irons in the punishment annex the POWs called Alcatraz. In 1969, chosen to be paraded in a propaganda film, Stockdale beat his own face with a stool and cut himself with a razor fragment rather than be used — he would be photographed battered or not at all. His captors understood the message: this man would die before he bent. In the aftermath, the worst of the torture campaign eased.

Stockdale came home in February 1973, pictured here descending from the aircraft a free man, and received the Medal of Honor in 1976. Eight years a prisoner, four of them in solitary — and the men he led credit his iron example with bringing them home alive, together, and unashamed. He died in 2005, an admiral, a philosopher of endurance, and the standard by which American POWs are still measured.

They put him on television to lie for them. Instead, blinking slowly, he told the whole world the truth. 🇺🇸

Commander Jeremiah Denton, a Navy A-6 Intruder pilot, was shot down over North Vietnam on July 18, 1965, and dragged into the prison system the Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. In May 1966, his captors sat him before Japanese television cameras for a propaganda interview, expecting a broken man to parrot their script.

Denton gave them the performance they wanted with his voice — while his eyes told a different story. As he spoke, he blinked, again and again, in Morse code: T-O-R-T-U-R-E. American intelligence officers studying the film caught it — the first proof the world had that American POWs were being tortured. It is one of the most extraordinary acts of defiance ever committed in front of an enemy's own camera.

Denton endured seven years and seven months of captivity, much of it in solitary and in the punishment camp the prisoners called Alcatraz, and came home in February 1973 — the first man off the plane at Clark Air Base, where he spoke for all of them: "We are honored to have had the opportunity to serve our country under difficult circumstances." He retired a Rear Admiral, served Alabama in the United States Senate, and died in 2014. The blink that outsmarted an empire still teaches every American service member what resistance means.

Starved to 98 pounds in a jungle prison, he crawled out of it — and then outran the jungle itself. 🇺🇸

Dieter Dengler grew up in the ruins of postwar Germany dreaming of American airplanes, crossed the ocean as a teenager, and earned his wings as a U.S. Navy pilot. On February 1, 1966, flying an A-1 Skyraider from the carrier Ranger on a secret mission over Laos, his plane was hit and crashed in the jungle. Dengler survived the crash — and walked straight into a Pathet Lao patrol.

What followed was months of torture: hung upside down, beaten, dragged, starved, staked to the ground in the camp as the prisoners wasted away. On June 29, 1966, the starving prisoners made their break. Dengler got out — one of only two of the escapees to survive the jungle — and then did the hardest part alone: 23 days evading recapture on foot, barefoot, eating what the wild offered, hiding from the men hunting him.

On July 20, 1966, an American Skyraider pilot spotted a signal on the jungle floor — a parachute laid out as an SOS by a man who refused to die — and helicopters pulled Dieter Dengler out, weighing less than 100 pounds, smiling for the cameras days later. He received the Navy Cross, flew again, and remains the only American airman to escape a Laotian prison camp and live to tell it.

He bombed Japan, rotted in its allies' cells for 40 months — then went back to Japan to love its people. 🇺🇸

Corporal Jacob DeShazer was the bombardier on the last plane of the Doolittle Raid, the daring carrier-launched strike on Tokyo of April 18, 1942. Out of fuel over occupied China, his crew bailed out into the night — straight into Japanese hands. Eight Raiders were captured; three were executed, one starved to death. DeShazer endured forty months of cells, hunger, disease and beatings, most of it in solitary confinement, not knowing if he would ever see Oregon again.

In that darkness, a smuggled Bible reached his cell — and DeShazer made a vow that sounds impossible: if he lived, he would return to Japan not with hatred, but as a missionary. He lived. Freed in August 1945, he kept the vow: in 1948 Jacob DeShazer went back to Japan and spent thirty years preaching to the people who had caged him.

A pamphlet telling his story fell into the hands of Mitsuo Fuchida — the commander who led the attack on Pearl Harbor. It helped change Fuchida's life; the two former enemies met, shook hands, and became friends. Jacob DeShazer died in 2008 at 95 — a POW who answered torture with the most disarming weapon ever carried into a prison camp: forgiveness.

In a historic ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit struck down core provisions of the 1958 Federal Switchblade Act, holding that automatically opening knives qualify as protected "Arms" under the plain text of the Second Amendment.

Dismantling a 1950s Ban: Enacted in 1958 amid 1950s pop-culture panics over juvenile delinquency, Section 1242 of the Federal Switchblade Act made it a federal crime to manufacture, transport, or sell automatic knives across state lines. The appellate panel found that the federal government failed to demonstrate any historical tradition justifying an interstate commercial ban.

Knives Are Constitutionally Protected "Arms": Applying the Supreme Court's historical-tradition framework, Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod wrote for the panel that bladed tools have been used for self-defense throughout American history. The court explicitly held that the right to keep and bear arms necessarily includes the right to manufacture, ship, and acquire them through interstate commerce.

What Changes (and What Doesn't): While the decision represents a major victory for pro-knife advocacy groups like Knife Rights and clears federal interstate trade barriers within the circuit, it does not automatically override individual state or municipal concealed-carry and blade-length statutes, which remain governed under separate local laws.

They called him unbroken — and after 47 days at sea and two years in the camps, the name fit. 🇺🇸

Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner from California who raced at the 1936 Berlin Games, and when war came he became a bombardier on a B-24 over the Pacific. On May 27, 1943, his crippled bomber, the Green Hornet, fell into the ocean during a rescue search. Zamperini and two crewmates survived on a tiny raft — drinking rain, catching fish and birds, fending off sharks — for 47 days, among the longest sea survivals in history. One of the three died on the raft. The other two washed up alive — straight into Japanese hands.

What followed was worse than the ocean: more than two years in prisoner-of-war camps, singled out for torment by a sadistic guard the prisoners called "the Bird," who beat the famous Olympian with a belt, starved him, and tried to break the thing in him that would not bend. It never broke. Zamperini came home in 1945 carrying nightmares that nearly destroyed him with drink — until, by his own account, faith put him back together, and the man who had every reason to hate flew back to Japan to forgive his captors face to face.

He died in 2014 at 97, a torch-bearer, a mentor to generations of young men, and the subject of the book and film "Unbroken." The title is not poetry. It is a description.

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. By July 2, 1863, he commanded the 20th Maine — and held the extreme left end of the entire Union line on Little Round Top at Gettysburg, with orders to hold "to the last." Among the officers beside him was his younger brother, Lieutenant Thomas Chamberlain.

All afternoon the 20th Maine beat back wave after wave of Alabamians climbing the rocks. Then the ammunition ran out. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. He was wounded so often in that war that newspapers printed his obituary by mistake; Grant chose him to formally receive the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, where Chamberlain ordered his men to salute their defeated enemies as they stacked their arms.

Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Two brothers of one Wisconsin family — and between them, two of the Civil War's most impossible feats. 🇺🇸

Alonzo Cushing, pictured here, was a 22-year-old artillery lieutenant whose battery stood at the very center of the Union line at Gettysburg — the stone wall called the Angle — on July 3, 1863. As Pickett's Charge rolled toward him, Alonzo was wounded again and again: a shell fragment through the shoulder, another through the body. Ordered to the rear, he refused, had himself held upright beside his last serviceable gun, and was sighting it with his thumb over the vent when a bullet struck him down at his post. The charge broke on the ground he would not leave. In November 2014 — 151 years later — President Barack Obama placed Alonzo Cushing's Medal of Honor where it had always belonged.

His younger brother needed no land battle for his legend. William Barker Cushing of the U.S. Navy, on the night of October 27, 1864, steamed a tiny launch with a spar torpedo up the dark Roanoke River, alone past Confederate guards, and detonated it beneath the ironclad CSS Albemarle — sinking the South's most feared warship and swimming for his life through icy water as it went down.

One brother held the line at the war's turning point. The other sank an ironclad in the dark. America has rarely asked more of one family's sons — and never received more.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

This is the true story behind Saving Private Ryan — and the truth is harder than the film. 🇺🇸

Four brothers from Tonawanda, New York, went to war: Edward, Preston, Robert and Frederick "Fritz" Niland. In one terrible June of 1944, the family's world collapsed. Robert, a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne, was k*lled on D-Day itself at Neuville-au-Plain. The very next day, June 7, Preston, also a paratrooper, fell near Utah Beach. And from the other side of the world came word that Edward, an airman whose plane had gone down in the Burmese jungle, was missing and presumed d*ad.

That left Fritz, fighting with the 101st Airborne in Normandy. When the Army realized three brothers were gone, it moved fast: the regimental chaplain, Father Francis Sampson, tracked Fritz down and the last Niland son was pulled from the line and sent home to his mother — the real "sole survivor" mission that Steven Spielberg later transformed into Saving Private Ryan.

And then, in 1945, came the telegram no one dared hope for: Edward was alive. Emaciated in a Japanese prison camp, he had survived. Two Niland brothers came home. Two rest side by side today in the American cemetery above Normandy — Preston and Robert, together, under white crosses in Plot B.

Five brothers. One ship. One night that changed America's rules of war forever. 🇺🇸

George, Francis, Joseph, Madison and Albert Sullivan were five Irish-American brothers from Waterloo, Iowa. When their friend Bill Ball was k*lled aboard the USS Arizona at Pearl Harbor, the brothers enlisted together — with one condition the Navy granted: they would serve together. All five were posted to the light cruiser USS Juneau, and their smiling photograph aboard her became one of the famous images of the young war.

On the night of November 13, 1942, in the savage naval battles off Guadalcanal, a Japanese torpedo struck the Juneau's magazine. She disintegrated and sank in less than a minute. Some hundred men survived the sinking and clung to rafts in shark-haunted water — but through a chain of communication failures, no rescue came for days. When help finally arrived, only ten men were pulled out alive. All five Sullivan brothers were gone.

Their mother Alleta received the news with a grace that humbled a nation, and their sister Genevieve joined the Navy's WAVES in their honor. The Navy named a destroyer USS The Sullivans — the only American warship ever named for a family — and the tragedy drove the military to separate siblings and protect sole surviving sons. "We stick together" was the brothers' motto. They did — to the very end.

Before there was a 75th Ranger Regiment, there was one young colonel in Scotland, building America's first Rangers from scratch. 🇺🇸

In the spring of 1942, with America reeling from defeats, Major William Orlando Darby — just 31 years old — was given a mission: create an American unit modeled on the legendary British Commandos. Five hundred volunteers were selected and shipped to Achnacarry, Scotland, where Commando instructors ran them through a course so brutal it used live ammunition. On June 19, 1942, the 1st Ranger Battalion was born — and Darby's men, pictured training here in those early days, were its standard-bearers.

That November, Rangers spearheaded the landings in North Africa, paddling ashore in darkness to silence the guns of Arzew. They fought through Sicily and Italy, at Gela and Salerno and Anzio — and at Cisterna, in January 1944, the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions walked into an ambush and were nearly annihilated: of 767 men who went in, only six came back.

Darby refused a safe job in Washington and returned to his men in Italy. On April 30, 1945, days before the war in Europe ended, a shell fragment took his life; he was promoted to Brigadier General on the day of his death. Today's Rangers still carry his name, his scroll, and his challenge — Darby's challenge — to lead the way. Rangers Lead The Way.

This U.S. soldier's M16A1 has one of the strangest attachments of the Vietnam War: the XM2 personnel detector, better known to the troops as the "People Sniffer." Developed by General Electric for the Army's Chemical Corps and fielded in 1967, it was built to find an enemy that was nearly impossible to see in thick jungle by detecting the chemical traces of human sweat and urine.

The system had a sensor carried in a backpack and an air intake tube mounted at the end of the rifle. Wherever the muzzle pointed, the device sampled the air. In theory, it would lead a patrol straight to a hidden enemy position.

In practice, troops found plenty of problems. The detector made noise, which is the last thing you want in an ambush position, and it was sensitive enough to pick up the sweat of the soldiers carrying it. The enemy also adapted quickly, reportedly hanging buckets of urine in the jungle to send the sniffers chasing ghosts. The airborne XM3 version mounted on helicopters saw much wider use, but the backpack model became a footnote.

It's a strange piece of gear and a reminder of how hard American troops worked to find an enemy who rarely wanted to be found.

The enemy kept a diary about them. One word appears again and again: the Black Devils. 🇺🇸

The First Special Service Force was an experiment no army had tried: one elite unit of Americans and Canadians, mixed together, trained for everything — parachuting, skiing, mountain climbing, amphibious raids, demolitions — at a secret camp in Montana under Colonel Robert Frederick.

In December 1943, at Monte la Difensa in Italy, the Force did what Allied planners called impossible: in a freezing night rainstorm, its men scaled a sheer cliff the Germans had left undefended precisely because no one could climb it — and took the summit fortress in two hours. At the Anzio beachhead, they owned the night: faces blackened, slipping into German lines to raid, sabotage and vanish, leaving behind their red spearhead sticker and a calling card in German: "Das dicke Ende kommt noch!" — "The worst is yet to come!"

A captured German officer's diary gave them their immortal name, describing an enemy that struck invisibly in the dark: "the Black Devils." The Force was disbanded in December 1944, its ranks shattered by casualties — but both nations' special forces trace their bloodline to it. The Devil's Brigade never lost a battle it was sent to win.

America locked their families behind barbed wire — then these sons volunteered to fight for it. 🇺🇸

After Pearl Harbor, more than 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced from their homes into internment camps. And from inside those camps, thousands of their sons stepped forward and volunteered for the United States Army. They became the 442nd Regimental Combat Team — fighting under a motto in Hawaiian pidgin: "Go For Broke."

In Italy and France, the 442nd built a legend battle by battle. In October 1944, in the freezing Vosges Mountains, they smashed through German lines to rescue the "Lost Battalion" — 211 trapped Texans of the 141st Infantry — at a cost of some 800 casualties of their own. Their artillerymen, like the 522nd Field Artillery gunners pictured here under their camouflage net, were famed for speed and precision — and in the spring of 1945, men of the 522nd were among the liberators who reached the sub-camps of Dachau.

For its size and length of service, the 442nd became the most decorated unit in United States Army history: more than 18,000 individual decorations, including 21 Medals of Honor. They had set out to prove their loyalty to a country that doubted it. They ended up proving something greater — what loyalty actually looks like.

They marched a thousand miles through jungle, fought an empire, and dissolved almost to the last man. 🇺🇸

In February 1944, some 3,000 American volunteers — jungle fighters, muleskinners, and men who spoke languages of the Pacific — slipped behind Japanese lines in Burma. Officially they were the 5307th Composite Unit. History knows them by their commander, Brigadier General Frank Merrill: Merrill's Marauders.

With only what they and their mules could carry, they marched farther than any American unit of the war — some 750 to 1,000 miles of mountain and jungle — and fought five major battles and dozens of skirmishes, cutting the supply lines of an army that outnumbered them many times over. Their true enemies were as much malaria, dysentery, and scrub typhus as the Japanese: men fought with fevers of 104 degrees, and the wounded who could walk were sent back to the line.

When the airfield at Myitkyina finally fell in August 1944, of the nearly 3,000 who had marched in, only about 200 remained fit for duty. Every Marauder received the Bronze Star, and in 2020 Congress awarded the unit its Gold Medal. Their legacy marches on today in the 75th Ranger Regiment, which carries the Marauders' lineage — and their impossible standard.

Their tanks were rubber. Their guns were dummies. And they saved thousands of lives. Meet the Ghost Army. 🇺🇸

In the summer of 1944, a strange unit landed in France: the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops — 1,100 men recruited not for their shooting, but for their sketchbooks. They were art students, designers, actors, architects and sound engineers, and their mission was pure deception: to impersonate entire American divisions — 30,000 men — with inflatable tanks, dummy aircraft, giant speakers blasting recorded sounds of armies on the move, and fake radio traffic.

Again and again, the Ghost Army set up its theater near the front while the real divisions slipped away to attack somewhere else. German reconnaissance saw the "tanks," heard the "army," and aimed at ghosts. Historians credit the unit with saving between 15,000 and 30,000 American lives — and then the whole story was classified for half a century. The artists never got their parade.

That finally changed on March 21, 2024, when the surviving Ghost Army veterans — most near a hundred years old — received the Congressional Gold Medal in Washington. One of their inflatable Sherman tanks, like the one pictured here, survives today in a museum: a balloon that helped win a war.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass. 

Conducted by researchers from the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine (USARIEM) and published in the Journal of Applied Physiology and Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, the study tracked male and female candidates through the 61+ days of severe caloric deprivation, minimal sleep, and non-stop physical exertion across the Darby, Mountain, and Swamp phases. 

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. It doesn't matter what your sex is."

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

One family. Six months. Four telegrams. 🇺🇸

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.
